lead: The 555 is an eight-pin IC that turns two resistors and one capacitor into a timer. Three 5 kΩ resistors set 2/3 V_CC and 1/3 V_CC; two comparators check a capacitor against them; a latch holds the result. It works as an astable oscillator, a monostable one-shot, a PWM generator and a missing-pulse alarm. It costs a few rupees and outputs about 200 mA.
prereq: You need multivibrators from Chapter 7.5 and comparators from Unit 6, Op-Amp Linear and Nonlinear Applications.

sections.h3: Inside the chip: three resistors, two comparators, one latch

blocks.text: Pin 1 is ground; pin 8 is V_CC (4.5 V to 16 V for the bipolar NE555). Pin 2 is TRIGGER, pin 6 is THRESHOLD, pin 7 is DISCHARGE, pin 3 is OUTPUT, pin 4 is RESET and pin 5 is CONTROL VOLTAGE.
Three identical 5 kΩ resistors from V_CC to ground fix 2/3 V_CC and 1/3 V_CC. The name 555 comes from them.
The upper comparator compares pin 6 with 2/3 V_CC and resets the latch above that level. The lower comparator compares pin 2 with 1/3 V_CC and sets the latch below that level.

The latch is an RS flip-flop. Its Q output drives an inverter and push-pull pair — sourcing or sinking about 200 mA for an LED or small relay — and the discharge transistor Q1, whose collector is pin 7. When Q is high, Q1 is on and pin 7 is grounded.

Pin 4 is active-low reset: tie it to V_CC, or pull it low to force the output low. Pin 5 exposes the 2/3 V_CC node; a voltage there moves the upper threshold, so a 10 nF capacitor from pin 5 to ground keeps noise off it.

sections.h3: Astable mode: charge through R_A + R_B, discharge through R_B

blocks.text: Connect R_A from V_CC to pin 7, R_B from pin 7 to pins 2 and 6 joined, and C from those pins to ground. If C starts below 1/3 V_CC, the lower comparator sets the latch: output high, Q1 off, C charges through R_A and R_B. At 2/3 V_CC the upper comparator resets the latch: output low, Q1 on, C discharges through R_B only into pin 7. At 1/3 V_CC the cycle restarts. The paths differ, so the half-periods differ.

blocks.where: T_H is output high time in seconds; R_A and R_B in ohms; C in farads; 0.693 = ln 2, the factor for charging from 1/3 V_CC to 2/3 V_CC.
T_L is output low time in seconds. Only R_B carries discharge current.

blocks.text: f = 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)   and   D = (R_A + R_B) / (R_A + 2 R_B)
blocks.where: f is in hertz; 1.44 ≈ 1/0.693; D is duty cycle, the fraction of the period high. R_A is in the charge path only, so T_H > T_L and D > 50%.

blocks.text: For D near 50%, connect a diode across R_B with anode at pin 7 and cathode at the pins 2/6 node. It bypasses R_B while C charges, so T_H ≈ 0.693 R_A C, while discharge still uses R_B, so T_L ≈ 0.693 R_B C. With R_A = R_B, D ≈ R_A/(R_A + R_B) = 50%.
Pick C first, from 1 nF to 10 µF, then solve for R_A and R_B. Keep R_B below about 1 MΩ; comparator bias current and capacitor leakage spoil long timings.

sections.h3: Monostable mode and the applications that follow

blocks.text: Connect R from V_CC to pin 7 and also to pin 6, C from pin 6 to ground, and leave pin 2 separate. A negative pulse on pin 2 below 1/3 V_CC sets the latch: output high, Q1 off, C charges through R. At 2/3 V_CC the latch resets and the output falls.

blocks.where: T is output pulse width in seconds; R in ohms; C in farads; 1.1 = ln 3, for charging from 0 V to 2/3 V_CC.

blocks.text: If the trigger stays below 1/3 V_CC longer than T, the lower comparator keeps setting the latch: the output goes high again immediately and repeats, so it keeps pulsing until the trigger is released. Keep the trigger shorter than T. Pin 4 stays at V_CC.

items: LED flasher: astable with R_A = 1 kΩ, R_B = 68 kΩ, C = 10 µF and an LED plus 470 Ω on pin 3 gives about a 1 Hz blink.
Tone generator: astable at audio frequency; pin 3 through a 100 µF or larger capacitor into an 8 Ω speaker, with a 100 Ω series resistor to limit pin 3 current.

Missing-pulse detector: each pulse triggers a monostable, so output stays high while pulses arrive; a missing pulse lets output fall low after T and drives the alarm. A plain 555 does not retrigger during T, so set T slightly longer than one pulse period and use a retriggerable arrangement, such as an extra discharge transistor. Useful in a UPI payment terminal watching a heartbeat line from the host.
PWM: a slowly varying voltage on pin 5 moves the upper threshold, changing T_H and the duty cycle while frequency stays roughly constant. This dims an LED or sets DC motor speed.

blocks.text: Tie pin 4 to V_CC directly or through 10 kΩ. An open pin 4 is bad practice on the bipolar NE555 — it usually runs — and unreliable on CMOS versions such as the 7555, where noise on the floating high-impedance input resets the timer at random and raises supply current.

figure.caption: The 555 signal path: the divider sets 2/3 V_CC and 1/3 V_CC, the comparators set and reset the latch, and the latch drives the discharge transistor on pin 7 and the output on pin 3.

spec.aria: The 555 internals from Vcc through the three-resistor divider to the two comparators, the flip-flop, the discharge transistor and the output stage.

examples.question: A 555 runs from V_CC = 9 V as an astable with R_A = 10 kΩ, R_B = 47 kΩ and C = 10 nF. (a) Find the two threshold voltages. (b) Find T_H, T_L, the period and the frequency. (c) Find the duty cycle. (d) The same R_B and C are rewired as a monostable with R = 47 kΩ; find the pulse width.
steps: (a) Upper threshold = 2/3 × 9 V = 6 V; lower threshold = 1/3 × 9 V = 3 V.
Charge path R_A + R_B = 57 kΩ, so T_H = 0.693 × 57 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.395 ms.
Discharge path R_B = 47 kΩ, so T_L = 0.693 × 47 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.326 ms.
D = T_H/T = 0.395/0.721 = 0.548, that is 54.8%. It is above 50% because R_A is in the charge path only.
Check: f = 1.44/((10 kΩ + 94 kΩ) × 10 nF) = 1385 Hz, within rounding.
examples.answer: T_H = 0.395 ms, T_L = 0.326 ms, T = 0.721 ms, f = 1388 Hz (about 1.39 kHz), duty cycle 54.8%, and the monostable pulse is 0.517 ms.
examples.check:
RA = 10e3
RB = 47e3
C = 10e-9
TH = 0.693 * (RA + RB) * C
TL = 0.693 * RB * C
T = TH + TL
f = 1 / T
duty = TH / T * 100
Tm = 1.1 * RB * C
print(round(TH * 1e3, 3))
print(round(TL * 1e3, 3))
print(round(T * 1e3, 3))
print(round(f))
print(round(duty, 1))
print(round(Tm * 1e3, 3))

traps: Assuming the two halves of the astable period are equal: charge uses R_A + R_B, discharge only R_B.
Using 0.693 R C for a monostable pulse: it charges 0 V to 2/3 V_CC, so use 1.1 R C.
Quoting D below 50% for the plain astable: D = (R_A + R_B)/(R_A + 2R_B) is always above 50%.
Leaving pin 4 open: tie it to V_CC; noise resets the timer, especially on CMOS.
Swapping R_A and R_B: R_A goes V_CC to pin 7; R_B from pin 7 to the capacitor node.

quiz.q: Which pin of the 555 senses the upper threshold, and at what fraction of V_CC does it switch?
quiz.a: Pin 6, THRESHOLD. Above 2/3 V_CC the upper comparator resets the latch.

quiz.q: Why is the duty cycle of the plain astable always greater than 50%?
quiz.a: C charges through R_A + R_B, so T_H = 0.693(R_A + R_B)C, but discharges through R_B alone, so T_L = 0.693 R_B C. The high time is longer; D = (R_A + R_B)/(R_A + 2R_B) exceeds 0.5.

quiz.q: An astable 555 has R_A = 1 kΩ, R_B = 68 kΩ and C = 1 µF. Find T_H, T_L, the frequency and the duty cycle.
A 555 monostable uses R = 100 kΩ and C = 10 µF. Find the output pulse width and state one condition on the trigger.
quiz.a: T = 1.1 R C = 1.1 × 100 kΩ × 10 µF = 1.1 s. The pin-2 trigger must be shorter than 1.1 s and dip below 1/3 V_CC = 3 V when V_CC = 9 V.

quiz.q: A 555 astable designed for 1 kHz measures 700 Hz on a breadboard. Give two plausible causes and say what measurement separates them.
quiz.a: The timing parts may be off value, V_CC may droop under load, the timing capacitor may leak, or pin 4 may float. Meter C and both resistors to test values and leakage; scope pin 3 with the load disconnected to check the supply and reset.

quiz.q: What does a slowly varying voltage on pin 5 do in a PWM application, and why?
quiz.a: It moves the upper comparator threshold away from 2/3 V_CC. A higher pin-5 voltage lengthens T_H and leaves discharge alone, so duty cycle rises; a lower voltage lowers it. Frequency changes only slightly, so it works as a dimmer or motor-speed control.

quiz.q: What happens if pin 4 is left unconnected?
quiz.a: On the bipolar NE555 it usually runs, because the reset input stays off open; it is still bad practice. On CMOS such as the 7555 the floating high-impedance input picks up noise and resets the timer at random, raising supply current. Tie pin 4 to V_CC directly or through 10 kΩ.

beyond: Not for the exam. CMOS versions (7555, TLC555) draw microamperes, not milliamperes, and suit battery devices. Microcontroller timers now replace the 555 in many products, but it survives in blinkers, fan controllers and kits because it needs no code. Pin 5 control leads to the VCO in Chapter 7.7.
